i: This Book takes its name from the holy man Tobit, whose wonderful virtues are herein recorded. It contains most excellent documents of great piety, extraordinary patience, and of a perfect resignation to the will of God. His humble prayer was heard, and the angel Raphael was sent to relieve him: he is thankful and praises the Lord, calling on the children of Israel to do the same. Having lived to the age of one hundred and two years, he exhorts his son and grandsons to piety, foretells the destruction of Nineveh and the rebuilding of Jerusalem: he dies happily.

a.1: Tobit's early piety: his works of mercy, particularly in burying the dead.
a.2: Tobit leaves his dinner to bury the dead: he loss his sight by God's permission, for manifestation of his patience.
a.3: The prayer of Tobit, and of Sarah, in their several afflictions, are heard by God, and the angel Raphael is sent to relieve them.
a.4: Tobit thinking he shall die, gives his son godly admonitions: and tells him of money he had lent to a friend.
a.5: Tobiah seeking a guide for his journey, the angel Raphael, in shape of a man, undertakes this office.
a.6: By the angel's advice Tobiah takes hold on a fish that assaults him. Reserveth the heart, the gall, and the liver for medicines. They lodge at the house of Raguel, whose daughter Sarah, Tobiah is to marry; she had before been married to seven husbands, who were all slain by a devil.
a.7: They are kindly entertained by Raguel. Tobiah demands Sarah to wife.
a.8: Tobiah burns part of the fish's liver, and Raphael binds the devil. Tobiah and Sarah pray.
a.9: The angel Raphael goes to Gabelus, receives the money, and brings him to the marriage.
a.10: The parents lament the long absence of their son Tobiah. He sets out to return.
a.11: Tobiah anoints his father's eyes with the fish's gall, and he recovers his sight.
a.13: Tobit praises God, exhorting all Israel to do the same. Prophesieth the restoration and better state of Jerusalem.
a.14: Tobit dies at the age of a hundred and two years, after exhorting his son and grandsons to piety, foreshewing that Nineveh shall be destroyed, and Jerusalem rebuilt.  Tobiah returns with his family to Raguel, and dies happily as he had lived.

2:15: Kings... So Job's three friends are here called, because they were princes in their respective territories.
3:7: Rages... In the Greek it is Ecbatana, which was also called Rages. For there were two cities in Media of the name of Rages. Raguel dwelt in one of them, and Gabelus in the other.
5:18: Azariah... The angel took the form of Azariah: and therefore might call himself by the name of the man whom he personated. Azariah, in Hebrew, signifies the help of God, and Ananias the grace of God.
6:8: Its heart, etc. The liver (ver. 19)... God was pleased to give these things a virtue against those proud spirits, to make them, who affected to be like the Most High, subject to such mean corporeal creatures as instruments of his power.
6:15: Hell... That is, to the place where the souls of the good were kept before the coming of Christ.
11:9: The dog, etc... This may seem a very minute circumstance to be recorded in sacred history: but as we learn from our Saviour, St. Matt. 5.18, there are iotas and tittles in the word of God: that is to say, things that appear minute, but which have indeed a deep and mysterious meaning in them.
13:11: Jerusalem... What is prophetically delivered here, and in the following chapter, with relation to Jerusalem, is partly to be understood of the rebuilding of the city after the captivity: and partly of the spiritual Jerusalem, which is the church of Christ, and the eternal Jerusalem in heaven.
